meanings.note: Possession, relationships and many fixed expressions.
Tener algo claro means to understand it or have a firm view of it.

examples.text: Tiene muy claro lo que quiere.
examples.trans: She is very clear about what she wants.

examples.text: Ha habido maricones toda la historia de la humanidad.

examples.trans: How did she do that by email?

examples.text: Que traigo un paquete para Belinda Washington.

examples.trans: I've brought a gift for you.

examples.text: ¡La tenemos! La voy a llamar y darle la sorpresa.
examples.trans: We've got her! I'm going to call her and give her the surprise.
Many thanks to all of you, everyone.

examples.text: Te llamo porque no localizo a Maqui.
examples.trans: I'm calling you because I can't reach Maqui.
I'm not going because I'm tired.

examples.text: Me depilo las piernas en casa.
examples.trans: I remove hair on my legs at home.

meanings.note: Understandable, evident, or settled in someone's mind in tener algo claro.
Links a clause after a judgment in the first lesson example; introduces a relative clause about people in the second.

examples.trans: I'm looking for people who work here.

meanings.note: Marks many specific human direct objects without a separate English word; in poco a poco it belongs to the expression little by little.
Stressed first-person singular pronoun after a preposition. Written with an accent, unlike possessive mi; may be doubled by unstressed me.
Unstressed first-person singular object; its exact direct/indirect/reflexive role depends on the verb.
Auxiliary before a past participle; does not express possession.
The impersonal present is hay, not ha.

examples.text: A mí me ha sorprendido mucho.
No hace falta que lo diga.
examples.trans: There is no need for me to say it.
I'm sure you look gorgeous, come out.
What time does she finish today?
She has a lot of talent.
Thank you very much for everything.
I get tiny red spots here.

examples.text: Tengo un granito en el brazo.
examples.trans: I have a tiny spot on my arm.

meanings.note: Identity, profession or a characteristic; compare estar for a state or location.

examples.text: No hace falta, la verdad. Vale.
Hablamos de falta en la oficina.
examples.trans: We talk about need, lack (hacer falta) at the office.

meanings.note: Also links tratar de + infinitive and forms more than with más de; these uses do not express possession.

examples.text: Llevo más de dos años aquí.
examples.trans: I've been here for more than two years.
That is a lack of exfoliation.
Exfoliation takes care of the skin.

examples.text: Me duele un poco el codo.

examples.trans: You have a very dry elbow.

examples.text: El aire de Madrid es seco.

meanings.note: A standalone answer can precede a separate negative statement, producing two occurrences of no.

examples.trans: She doesn't have a single wrinkle.

examples.text: Te llamo la semana que viene.

meanings.note: With a gerund, presents an action developing over time.

examples.text: Poco a poco hemos ido mejorando.
Ser buena persona es una cosa bonita en la vida.
examples.trans: Being a good person is a lovely thing in life.

examples.text: ¿Qué haces aquí? Que no me has avisado ni me has escrito.
De un corto. Era un escaparate muy bueno.
examples.trans: For a short film. It was a really good showcase.

examples.text: Pues yo veo muchos cortos, y aquel era buenísimo.
examples.trans: Well, I watch lots of short films, and that one was brilliant.

examples.text: Además es un corto precioso sobre una madre joven que lo pasa fatal.
examples.trans: Besides, it's a lovely short film about a young mother having a terrible time.
It is a critique of television.
It is a critique for television.
She works a lot in television.

meanings.note: Subject pronoun; often omitted when the verb already identifies the person.
Before a noun it is a determiner; standing alone, todos/todas can mean everyone or all of them.

examples.text: Salgo yo sola todo el rato.
examples.trans: It's just me the whole time.

examples.text: Hablamos un rato en la calle.
examples.trans: We chatted for a while in the street.

examples.text: Es buena en drama y es buena en comedia.
examples.trans: She is good at drama and she is good at comedy.

examples.text: Muy de moda ese papel. ¿Y por qué lloras, corazón?
examples.trans: That kind of role is very in style. And why are you crying, sweetheart?

examples.text: Que no lloro, es que estoy un poco agobiada.
examples.trans: I'm not crying, I'm just a bit overwhelmed.

examples.text: Cualquier día estás ahí tú, y yo aquí mirándote. No llores más.
examples.trans: Any day now you'll be up there, and I'll be right here watching you. Don't cry anymore.

examples.text: Para todo. Desde luego me gusta un montón y hace reír.
examples.trans: For everything. I definitely like him a lot and he makes people laugh.

examples.text: Hablamos de reír en la oficina.
examples.trans: We talk about to laugh at the office.

examples.text: Solamente necesita querer. Y querer es poder, eso está claro, Paquita.
examples.trans: You only need to want it. And where there's a will there's a way, that's clear, Paquita.

examples.text: Todos me han dicho que tú estás muy pasada de moda, que necesito un cambio.
examples.trans: Everyone has told me you're really out of date, and that I need a change.

examples.text: Es que tengo una actriz que necesito que veas. Se llama Lidia San José.

meanings.note: In estar bien or estar mal, evaluates an action or situation.

examples.trans: I can't do it on my own.
It's difficult, but I can do it.
I want to go, but I am working.

meanings.note: Normally a singular collective in this meaning. The plural gentes exists, especially in other or literary uses; ordinary English people is not a reason to make the Spanish verb plural.

examples.trans: There are a lot of people.
Can you check that socket for me?
